summary: Specifies attribute types and object classes for LDAP directory clients, for services such as white pages. They are widely used as the basis for schemas in many directories. It does not cover server administration. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4519 defines standard fields and entry types for information in LDAP directories. It helps directory clients agree on how to describe people, organizations, places, and groups.

subtitle: Standard LDAP fields and entry types for people, organizations, and groups.

tldr.problem: LDAP directory clients need shared definitions for common information about people, organizations, locations, and groups.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines 43 attribute types and 14 object classes, with names, identifiers, syntaxes, matching rules, and required or optional attributes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4519 replaces RFC 2256 and is the definitive description of these schema elements for LDAP. It updates RFCs 2247, 2377, and 2798.

today: RFC 4519 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006 and obsoletes RFC 2256. It updates RFC 2247, RFC 2377, and RFC 2798.

sections.title: Scope and Related LDAP Documents
sections.content:
This RFC specifies attribute types and object classes for LDAP clients that use directory services such as White Pages. These definitions are based mainly on X.500 schema and are widely used as a basis for LDAP directory schemas.

It does not define fields for administering directory servers or objects defined for specialized uses elsewhere. RFC 4519 replaces RFC 2256; related syntax and matching-rule material is in RFC 4517, and directory information models are in RFC 4512.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defines common data fields and entry types for LDAP directories. It does not define every kind of directory data or server administration field.

sections.title: Attribute Types for Directory Entries
sections.content:
The RFC defines 43 attribute types for information stored in entries. Each definition gives a name, an object identifier, a syntax, matching rules where applicable, and examples.

Examples include cn for an object's name, sn for a family name, telephoneNumber for a telephone number, and postalAddress for an address. The dc attribute holds one DNS domain label, such as example, not a complete name such as example.com.

Servers SHOULD recognize the defined attributes except searchGuide and teletexTerminalIdentifier, whose use is greatly discouraged and which servers need not implement. Clients MUST NOT assume that servers support attribute subtyping.
sections.plainLanguage: An attribute type names one kind of information that an entry can hold, such as a person's name or phone number. The RFC defines what values each field can contain.

sections.title: Object Classes and Required Attributes
sections.content:
An object class describes what kind of entry a directory record represents and which attributes it MUST or MAY contain. The RFC defines 14 classes, and servers SHOULD recognize them as values of objectClass.

For example, a person entry MUST have sn and cn. An organization entry MUST have o, while an organizationalUnit entry MUST have ou.

groupOfNames requires a common name and member values; groupOfUniqueNames uses unique member names. The auxiliary classes dcObject and uidObject add domain-component or user-ID information to another structural class.
sections.plainLanguage: An object class says what an entry represents and which fields it must contain. A person entry and an organization entry therefore have different required fields.

sections.title: Privacy and Password Handling
sections.content:
Directory attributes describe real people, organizations, and devices. The RFC notes that many countries have privacy laws concerning publication of information about people.

The userPassword attribute stores octet strings and does not encrypt them. Textual passwords SHOULD be converted to Unicode, prepared with SASLprep, and encoded as UTF-8. Sending cleartext passwords is strongly discouraged when the transport cannot protect confidentiality and integrity.

Multiple values need care because an administrator who does not know the old password may have difficulty replacing or deleting values. For authentication, a user needs to prove knowledge of one stored value, not all of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The password field does not encrypt a password, so the connection must protect it during transfer. Keeping several password values can also make password changes harder.

sections.title: LDAP Descriptor Registry
sections.content:
IANA updated the LDAP descriptors registry so the short names in this document refer to RFC 4519. The registry records whether a name identifies an attribute or an object class and gives its object identifier.

The document includes alternate names such as commonName, domainComponent, surname, and userid. Names reserved without an assigned object identifier are listed as RESERVED.
sections.plainLanguage: The LDAP descriptor registry records the names and identifiers for these fields and classes. RFC 4519 updates the registry entries to point to this specification.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2256
sections.content:
The update moved syntaxes and matching rules to RFC 4517 and directory information model material to RFC 4512. It moved certificate-related schema to RFC 4523 and removed several other older definitions.

RFC 4519 adds security and IANA sections, explanations and examples for schema elements, and definitions for dc, dcObject, and uidObject. The appendix identifies these changes as informational.
sections.plainLanguage: The revision moved some material to companion RFCs and removed schema that no longer belongs here. It also added explanations, examples, and updated definitions.
